title: West Sikkim monastery circuit: from Yuksom to Namchi
meta_description: The West and South Sikkim monastery circuit: Dubdi, Pemayangtse, Tashiding, Rinchenpong, Ralang and more, with etiquette and a 4–6 day jeep plan.
summary: West and South Sikkim hold the oldest monasteries in the state: Dubdi, Sanga Choeling, Pemayangtse and Tashiding, all tied to the 1642 coronation at Yuksom. By shared jeep or a hired car you can see the main ones in 4–6 days, basing yourself at Pelling, Yuksom and Ravangla. Entry is free or small.

sections.heading: Why these monasteries belong together
paras: In 1642 three lamas who had come over the passes from Tibet met at Yuksom and consecrated Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal, or dharma king, of Sikkim. The stone throne where that happened still stands at Norbugang, and almost every old monastery in this part of Sikkim traces itself back to that moment or to the lamas involved. Lhatsun Chempo, the senior of the three, is linked to Dubdi, Sanga Choeling and Pemayangtse; Ngadak Sempa Chempo founded Tashiding. Together they form the first map of Sikkimese Buddhism, laid out across one valley system.

Most of these are Nyingma monasteries, the oldest school of Tibetan Buddhism, which looks to Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava). Tradition holds that he blessed the whole region as Demazong, the hidden valley of rice, and you will hear that name often. Further south, around Ravangla and Namchi, the circuit adds newer sites: a Kagyu monastery at Ralang, the large Buddha at Rabong and the Guru Rinpoche statue at Samdruptse, built in the last thirty years but already major pilgrim stops.

sections.heading: Yuksom: Norbugang and Dubdi
paras: Start where the story starts. Norbugang Coronation Throne is a short walk from Yuksom bazaar: a stone seat for the Chogyal, smaller seats for the lamas, a chorten and an old pine tree that the local story says grew from the spot. A few minutes away, Kathok Lake is a still pond whose water was traditionally used in consecration rites. Above the village, Tashi Tenka is the site of the old palace, now little more than a terrace and a view.

Dubdi Monastery, built in 1701 under the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, is often called the oldest monastery in Sikkim. It sits on a ridge about 45 minutes of steep stone steps and forest path above Yuksom, and the climb is part of the visit. The building is small and plain, often locked when the caretaker monk is away, so go in the morning and ask in the village whether someone is up there. Leave a donation of ₹20–50 and close the gate behind you.

sections.heading: The Pelling ridge: three monasteries in a day
paras: Pemayangtse, whose name is usually given as perfect sublime lotus, was founded around 1705 by Lhatsun Chempo's lineage. It was the monastery whose head lama anointed the Chogyals, and by tradition its monks came only from ta-sang, or pure, Bhutia families. Climb to the top floor for Zangdok Palri, a seven-tiered painted wooden model of Guru Rinpoche's celestial palace that Dungzin Rinpoche is said to have carved over about five years. Entry is around ₹20–50 and photography inside is not allowed.

From near Pemayangtse a forest path of 15–20 minutes leads to the ruins of Rabdentse, Sikkim's capital from 1670 until Gorkha raids pushed the court to Tumlong in the early 1800s. Walls, chortens and a stone platform remain, with Kanchenjunga beyond on a clear morning. Sanga Choeling, established in 1697 and among the oldest monasteries in Sikkim, crowns the ridge above Pelling: allow 40 minutes uphill on foot, or drive most of the way to the Chenrezig statue and skywalk that opened nearby in 2018.

sections.heading: Khecheopalri Lake and Tashiding
paras: Khecheopalri is a lake rather than a monastery, but no pilgrim skips it. It is sacred to Buddhists and Hindus, its older name Sho Dzo Sho is explained as O lady, sit here, and the local story is that birds pick up any leaf that lands on the water. A prayer-flag jetty runs out over the edge; there is no boating or fishing, and voices drop without anyone asking. The small Khecheopalri gompa sits in the village on the hill above, a 30-minute walk up.

Tashiding Monastery stands on a heart-shaped hill between the Rathong Chu and the Rangeet. Ngadak Sempa Chempo founded it in 1641 and it was enlarged in 1717 under the third Chogyal. Walk the rows of carved mani stones to the Thongwa Rangdol chorten, said to cleanse sins by sight alone. If you can come for Bumchu in February or March, you will see the sacred vase opened and its water read as a forecast for the year. Expect a 20–30 minute climb from the road.

sections.heading: Rinchenpong, Ralang, Ravangla and Namchi
paras: Rinchenpong Monastery, built in 1730 on a hill above the village, keeps a rare image of Adi Buddha, Kuntuzangpo, in yab-yum, the union of male and female. It is quiet, small and worth the 2-hour drive from Pelling, especially if you stay a night at Rinchenpong or Kaluk for the dawn view of Kanchenjunga.

Around Ravangla the mood changes from old wood to new scale. Buddha Park, also called Tathagata Tsal, holds a Buddha about 40 m (130 ft) high, consecrated by the Dalai Lama in 2013, with Rabong Gompa beside it. About 13 km away, the new Ralang Palchen Choeling is a large Kagyu monastery built in the 1990s, and the much older Ralang gompa stands a short way above it. At Namchi, the 36 m Guru Padmasambhava statue on Samdruptse hill was completed in 2004 and faces Kanchenjunga across the valleys.
list: Buddha Park entry: around ₹50–100 for Indians; check current fees at the gate.
Samdruptse: about 7 km from Namchi bazaar; take a shared or reserved taxi up and walk down if you like.
Ralang: easiest by reserved taxi from Ravangla, about ₹800–1,200 return with waiting time.

sections.heading: Monastery etiquette
paras: These are working monasteries, not museums. Young monks study, cook, sweep and play cricket in the courtyards, and older lamas keep a daily round of prayers that began long before visitors came by car. Most are glad to see you and will open a hall or point out a mural if you ask politely, often in Nepali or Hindi. A few simple habits make that welcome easy, and they are the same at a famous gompa like Pemayangtse as at a village shrine where the caretaker has to fetch the key from his house.
list: Walk clockwise around monasteries, chortens, prayer wheels and mani walls, always keeping them on your right.
Take off shoes and hats before entering a prayer hall, and keep your voice low.
Cover shoulders and knees. A light shawl solves most problems for men and women.
Ask before photographing inside; at Pemayangtse and many others it is not allowed at all. Never use flash near murals.
Do not touch statues, butter lamps or ritual objects, and never sit with your feet pointing towards the altar.
Do not climb on chortens, sit on mani walls or step over monks' cushions and texts.
If a puja is on, stand at the back or wait outside; leaving quietly is better than filming.
A small offering of ₹10–50 in the donation box, or a white khada scarf, is welcome but never required.
Drones need permission and are usually refused near religious sites.

sections.heading: How to sequence it by jeep in 4–6 days
paras: Distances are short on the map and slow on the road, so the trick is to base yourself in three places and do day loops. Shared jeeps link Jorethang, Gyalshing, Pelling, Yuksom, Tashiding and Ravangla, mostly leaving in the morning, with seats from ₹40–60 on short hops to ₹150–250 on longer ones. For days with several stops, a reserved car from Pelling costs about ₹2,500–3,500 for local sightseeing. The six-day plan below starts from Siliguri and ends at Pelling or Rinchenpong.

list: Four days: skip Namchi and Ravangla, and do Yuksom, Khecheopalri, Tashiding and the Pelling ridge, with Rinchenpong on the way out.
Five days: add Ravangla and Ralang, coming in via Jorethang and leaving via Pelling.
Start each day early: monasteries are most alive at the morning puja, between about 6 and 8 am, and roads are clearer before noon.

faqs.q: Which is the oldest monastery in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Dubdi Monastery above Yuksom, built in 1701 under Chogyal Chakdor Namgyal, is the one most often called the oldest. Tashiding traces its founding to 1641 and Sanga Choeling to 1697, so the answer depends on whether you count a foundation or a surviving building. All three are in West Sikkim and easy to combine in a few days.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for the West Sikkim monastery circuit?
faqs.a: Four days covers the core: Yuksom with Norbugang and Dubdi, Khecheopalri Lake, Tashiding and the Pelling ridge with Pemayangtse, Rabdentse and Sanga Choeling. Six days lets you add Rinchenpong in the west and Ravangla, Ralang and Namchi in the south without rushing, which matters because hill roads here average 20–25 km an hour.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Pemayangtse Monastery?
faqs.a: Yes, a small one, usually around ₹20–50 for Indian visitors, collected at the gate. Photography inside the prayer halls is not allowed, and the top floor with the Zangdok Palri model may be closed during rituals. Fees are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel and carry small notes.

faqs.q: What should I wear to visit monasteries in Sikkim?
faqs.a: Clothes that cover shoulders and knees, and shoes you can slip off quickly at the door of each prayer hall. Remove hats inside. Mornings are cold at 2,000 m even in April, so a jacket or shawl is useful. There is no rule against jeans or trousers for women, but very short shorts and sleeveless tops draw looks.

faqs.q: Can I visit the monasteries by shared jeep?
faqs.a: Mostly, yes. Shared jeeps run between Jorethang, Gyalshing, Pelling, Yuksom, Tashiding and Ravangla, leaving mostly in the morning. Fares run from ₹40–60 for short hops to ₹150–250 for longer legs. You will walk the last stretch to Dubdi, Sanga Choeling and Tashiding anyway. For days with many stops, a reserved car at ₹2,500–3,500 saves hours.

faqs.q: When is the best time to see monastery festivals?
faqs.a: February and March, when Pemayangtse holds its cham masked dances before Losar and Tashiding hosts Bumchu, the reading of the sacred vase. August and September bring Pang Lhabsol, which Ravangla celebrates on a large scale. Dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar and move each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Sikkim monasteries?
faqs.a: Usually not inside the prayer halls, and never with flash, because light damages old murals and thangkas. Courtyards, exteriors and views are fine. Always ask a monk or caretaker before photographing people or rituals, and put the camera away if a puja is under way. Drones need permission and are usually refused near religious sites.

faqs.q: Is the Rabdentse ruin worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like history in quiet places. Rabdentse was Sikkim's capital from 1670 until Gorkha raids forced the court to move to Tumlong in the early 1800s. A 15–20 minute forest path from near Pemayangtse leads to the walls, chortens and a stone platform with a mountain view. Go early, when the gate opens and the light is soft.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for the monastery circuit?
faqs.a: Base yourself at Pelling for the ridge monasteries and Khecheopalri, Yuksom for Norbugang, Dubdi and Tashiding, and Ravangla for Buddha Park and Ralang. Pelling has budget rooms from about ₹1,200–2,500, and Yuksom and Ravangla have family guesthouses and homestays at ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast.
